title: Mineral Reference Standards for EPMA-WDS and SEM-EDS: Instrumental Calibration, Standards Comparison, and Quality Control
content: A previous critique of microanalysis reference standards used “Good” for materials with wet chemistry and other non-EPMA characterization, “Bad” for materials with only EPMA or no characterization, and “Ugly” for materials with oxidized surfaces and other sins of improper standard curation [1]. Existing microanalysis standards include natural and synthetic mineral and glass materials from the Smithsonian Institution mineral collection (SMS) [2]. Commercial mounts have included samples obtained from the Stanford University mineral collection. The SMS standards have independent wet chemistry analyses from the master grain separate as well as sigma ratio measurements of intra- and inter-grain variability. Most commercial mineral standards are provided with best estimate compositions that range from presumed stoichiometry (i.e., “CaF2”) to analyses obtained by EPMA-WDS or standardless EDS. Experienced analysts understand the importance of using high-concentration, stoichiometric and/or well-characterized reference standards for primary calibration, subsequent analysis of true secondary standards to verify analytical accuracy, and analysis of trace element and blank standards to verify low-level accuracy, the detection limit, and zero-concentration backgrounds. The prevalence of standardless EDS analysis used on SEMs in many laboratories has apparently resulted in a lack of verification using conventional standards. The Microanalysis Society as a leadership organization, coupled with efforts from the microanalysis community, is helping to identify new standard materials in addition to characterizing existing reference standards.
